I want to start this review by saying that I love this game. I've run hundreds and thousands of auric level mission, I've maxed out the levels of both base and DLC classes, I was even there when you only get one talent point for every 5 levels, when the weapon system overhaul was implemented, and even when the penance system was introduced. I've powered through all the bullsh*t for more than 3 years and over, thinking "fatshark will fix this soon," They didn't. Many aspect of the game has improved over the years, but it does not excuse them for doing a poor management of addressing these issues for this long:

>unbalanced engagement - by far my biggest gripe about the game. The game presents you with a TON of weapons for you to play with for both ranged and melee options, and yet 80% of said weapons will never see daylight because fatshark decided that spamming armoured enemies is the definition of hard: there are many types of enemies present in the game: unarmoured, unyielding, maniac, flak and carapace makes up most of the priority enemies that the game will throw at you. Some weapon are better at dealing with certain types of enemies, and are weaker at handling other types of enemies compared to the other weapons at your disposal. However, this wouldn't have been an issue if CARAPACE type enemies wasn't so prominent/oppresive in the game; carapace type enemies usually have some parts if not all of their body to be covered in heavy plate armour, and these armours can only be bypassed through a handful of weapons, while the rest of the weapon will LITTERALY bounce off from making contact with the armour. And since the game will spam these guys at you at higher levels, bringing a non-carapace weapon for both your melee and ranged slot will often means you kiting those fuckers continuously while slowly chipping away at their health, or praying for a teammate to help you. They said that they have reduced the number of carapace armour enemies, but with anti-armour weapons nerfs and carapace enemies still spawn in droves, I do not feel that much difference in engagement.

>audio issues - my second biggest gripe of this game, right above network and connectivity issues. Audio cue plays an essential role in this game; melee and/or ranged attacks of enemies are announced with a unique audio cue to tell you when an attack is directed towards you, and all specialist and elite enemies will have a unique audio cue that plays out whenever they're present on the field and when they're going to attack. so be it during ranged or melee combat, you can have time to react to their attacks even if you can't see them. The problem arises when these cues failed to play out before the enemy's attack: when enough enemy spawn and/or alive in the area that you're team are currently in, some audio will fail to play out correctly, or not play out at all. The amount of times I got blown up by a poxbursters because I didn't hear it's ticking amongst the horde, or the times I got downed from a silent trapper, dog or sniper have probably made up more than 50% of my total deaths.

>enemies spawning behind you - and no, this is not because I didn't check my surroundings or because I was standing near their spawn door: You could be in the middle of an open field - no spawn doors in sight and in between your teammates - and saw a horde coming your way. You pulled out your ranged weapon to pick them off and all of the sudden you get hit in the back. You turn around and see some SMUCKS just spawned from THIN-F*CKIN-AIR, RIGHT BETWEEN YOUR BACK AND YOUR TEAMATES, just to hit you. This is where some people would say "git gud" but in my honest opinion, it just makes any engagement more of a chore than anything: spawning enemies behind player doesn't add challenge to the game, but instead it punishes player for not playing like a spazzed-out crackhead. It's a cheap way of adding unnecessary tension to an already brutal combat, and it just makes any fight more frustrating than rewarding. In the higher levels, a singular horde mob only needs a couple of swings to down you. That's why damage reduction and toughness nodes are so important to any operatives. But because of these guys could spawn behind your character at any given time, they can whittle you down by stacking unnecessary damage onto your toughness and health, which opens you up to other attacks. They also body block your operatives (excluding ogryn) since enemy collision is a thing, so when you're trying to make some space between you and that wall of crushers heading towards you, don't be surprised when all of the sudden you just stopped moving.

All of this without mentioning the jankiness of some elites/specialist enemies, a big file size of nearly 100GBs, predatory microtransaction store that they refuse to do anything about even with many players asking it to be removed, long gaps between updates, the game chugging from time to time, ranged and melee hits sometimes just won't register, silent footsteps for enemies that aren't SUPPOSED to be silent, lazy event rewards which are nothing more than fancy picture frames, crashing, disconnecting and a myriad of other issues that continues to stack up with one another.

This game have so much potential to be a really great horde shooter, and it is disheartening to see it being handled as so. Especially when one of their older game "vermintide 2" have fixed or even somewhat addressed much of the issues mentioned. I don't know why those system aren't implemented into this game but until then, if you decide to buy this game still, you'll have to bear it until god knows when.

The technical issues alone are enough for a not recommended, but those can be fixed. My main issues are with everything else. The central hub is way too big for how little there is to do in it. It could easily be condensed down for the sake of player convenience. I don't even think there's a target dummy to test weapons, and you're in third person for some reason. There's no options for solo play whatsoever with bots. You can't have private lobbies. If you group up with some friends, you can't see them in the hub. In-game stats, icons, perks, etc. are poorly explained or not explained at all. What is finesse, for example? Why are values displayed as bars instead of actual numbers? What are those three icons shown on every weapon? What do they indicate? There are no weapon modifications. The game relies on the incredibly boring and lazy gear score system as a quick way to crank out 1000 different variants of the exact same weapons with only minor stat differences. The loadout only consists of melee weapon and ranged weapon, neither of which can be customized from what I could see. They only brought back trinkets from Vermintide, called curios. It's pretty barebones. No options for armor or different special abilities to help give customization some more depth. There are cosmetic appearance changes which I'm cool with, but that's just the icing on the cake. It doesn't effect gameplay. 

Missions are randomly generated in the mission terminal and you're given a time window to complete it before it's replaced with something else. This makes little sense to me since levels themselves are not really procedurally generated. This works better in a game like Deep Rock Galactic where no two levels are the same. The 6 different missions I've played in the beta have all been pretty repetitive due to samey objectives typically boiling down to fetch quests and push button and wait while enemies attack you objectives. I don't get the point of having a prologue sequence before a forced tutorial. Shouldn't it be the other way around or just merged into one, so we can get to grinding as soon as possible? Expect to grind as main overall objectives will require you to just repeatedly play missions til you hit a certain trust level to progress.

Classes aren't distinct enough in my opinion. The Ogryn is the most unique visually, but the Psyker is the most unique mechanically, but was unfortunately nerfed heavily from the closed beta. I get they want to balance this class, but the class was great because it was essentially a glass cannon. Now it's just a glass pistol. Still viable, but not as powerful due to the increased peril gains across their entire kit. I main the Zealot, and he's just boring. His main special is his rush ability that just ain't all that great on its own until you level up and get some better perks to buff it. Class progression is lackluster since there are impressively 18 traits you unlock three at a time, but you can only choose six to be active and they all lack character. They're mostly based on chance or some specific parameter that has to be met to be activated and only for a few seconds. They're just boring perks that don't make my Zealot feel that much different. It's all passive with little to no active perks. Many of the weapons aren't even class specific making classes feel even less distinct. Psykers and Zealots share ranged and melee weapons, for example. I'm not asking for more classes. I'm asking for more class customization options. Shops rotate weapons every hour and the requisitorium you unlock at a higher level is just a weekly challenge vendor to earn special currency to unlock higher tier weapons. Loot sucks in this game. It's even more shallow than Vermintide.

Most melee weapons' "special attack" is completely useless. Melee combat is pretty satisfying in the blood/gore, impact, and sound, but it's pretty shallow overall. Stamina management is a bit of an after thought as well since you can get away with spamming left click and occasionally block shoving. Ranged combat is better, but has problems. Ranged enemies are all hitscan and get guaranteed hits on you so long as a part of your body is visible. I've seen these dudes pop me through the slits of a staircase. They're super accurate with the lasrifle, but the lasrifle you get (along with most other guns) is just not that accurate at long range. Also, I love the game's presentation, but the added fog effect makes enemies hard to see at a distance. Don't be deceived by all the guns, this is a melee game first and foremost. I don't think they mixed the two all that well. Every mission I've played here and in the closed beta are melee-focused with ammo being pretty scarce. I think they could break up the monotony by having shooting-focused missions, melee-focused missions, and missions that mix the two. As of right now, the game will have numerous sequences where you're constantly attacked by endless hordes of melee and ranged enemies while giving you very little ammo til you complete your objective. Enemy spawns can be a real chore as they can easily spawn in behind you giving little indication an enemy was even in the vicinity. For example, while playing a difficulty 3 or 4 mission, I used a med bay to fully heal myself only for, seconds later, an exploding enemy to emerge from the door behind me and knock out half my health. There's a reason L4D had safe rooms. Teamwork is barely encouraged leading to most matches being with players not using a mic, grabbing all items for themselves, or just leaving players behind to fend for themselves. Add more abilities that buff the team in some way to encourage teamwork.

TL;DR
Moving from A to B on a map while dodging, blocking, hitting, and shooting everything in your way. The 'Tide gameplay loop and soundtrack never get old. It’s more ranged-focused than the Vermintide games, yet more melee-focused than Left 4 Dead. Let down by inconsistent performance, half-baked game modes, limited cosmetics, and a desperate need for more maps in the core mode.

Player Context
Coming from nearly 2,000 hours across both Vermintide games, the muscle memory was already there, but Darktide shifts the formula. Vermintide was at core melee-focused, with limited ammunition reserved for specials while you carved through chaff up close. Darktide leans much more heavily into gunplay. Almost a 50/50 split. It’s faster, more frantic, and constantly pushes you forwards. You’re almost always dodging, sliding, and charging into the next map set piece.

Combat
The gameplay itself isn’t especially varied, but the shooting, melee combat, and movement all feel excellent. You and three teammates fight through missions, dealing with hordes and specialist enemies, scavenging ammo and health, reviving each other, and pushing through objectives. Enemies explode, are decapitated, sliced apart, burned alive, thrown into bottomless pits, or riddled with bullets. Every weapon feels satisfying to use, and even better to hear. The four core classes offer distinct playstyles through abilities, talent trees, stats, and weapon choices. Instead of Vermintide’s named heroes, you create your own Reject by choosing background, appearance, voice, height, tattoos, and more. It should give more ownership over your character, but face and hairstyle options are limited, so you often run into near-identical characters. Most armour hides tattoos anyway. Free cosmetics earned through challenges or currency are generally good, but the premium shop rotates stock purely to create FOMO. Some outfits clip badly, while others are barely distinguishable from existing sets. As of writing, neither the Hive Scum nor Arbites classes have received any new cosmetics since release.

Reaching level 30 with each class doesn’t take long, but upgrading your armoury can feel like a grind. New players are heavily limited by crafting resources needed for weapon upgrades and blessing management. Weapon balance is in a good place overall. Some options are clearly stronger, but almost everything is viable on high difficulties with the right build. You don’t need to chase the meta—if a weapon feels good, it’ll work.

The enemy armour system was one of the more intimidating mechanics early on when I started. Instead of a simple light/heavy setup, enemies have different armour types, and sometimes across different body parts. A charged Voidstrike Staff shot might do great damage against a carapace wearing Crusher, but feel weak against a shirtless Mutant, who has a completely different armour profile from similarly near-nude enemies like Infested or Poxbursters. Expect to spend time in the Testing Grounds to figure this out.

Maps
The maps are gorgeous and do an excellent job of showing life inside the Tertium Hive. Like Left 4 Dead and Vermintide, the AI Director keeps repeat runs fresh by varying spawns and encounters. They’re really fantastic maps, I just wish there were more of them!

Since release, Fatshark has added a few new maps, but recent updates have focused more on additional game modes. Auric and Havoc provide harder versions of existing missions, while Mortis Trials and Expeditions offer new ways to play. If you’ve played Vermintide 2’s Chaos Wastes, these modes feel like someone split its best ideas in half. Mortis Trials is a wave survival mode where you fight through nine increasingly difficult rounds, choosing boons after each wave to create ridiculous builds. It’s fun, but limited by only three maps, and it lacks the journey and exploration that made Chaos Wastes so good. Expeditions are extraction runs outside the Hive City. You explore semi-randomised maps, gather Tech-Remnants, and extract when you choose. Leave early for modest rewards, or push further for more. Despite randomisation, runs start to feel very similar, and the mode would benefit heavily from Mortis-style modifiers.

Performance & Networking
Matchmaking in the UK has been solid for core missions at all difficulties. However, Mortis Trials and Expeditions have noticeably longer queues, which raises questions about their long-term population. Performance and optimisation still need work. Lowering settings makes surprisingly little difference to visuals or FPS. On my system, the game on Windows 11 delivers a fairly stable 80–90 FPS, while Linux sits in the high 70s, both with poor 1% lows. For Linux players on Nvidia GPUs, ray tracing is currently broken and can cause crashes. Ray tracing works fine on Windows, but isn’t worth the performance hit imo.

Music
I left the second best part for last: the music and sound design. Do yourself a favour, listen to Imperial Advance, Light of the Imperium, and Disposal Unit (Imperium Mix) on YouTube — you’ll hear them constantly in-game, and they never get old. Jesper Kyd’s soundtrack is excellent throughout. Weapons sound heavy and dangerous, melee hits land with real weight, and every elite or specialist enemy has distinct audio cues that cut through even the chaos of hordes. The audio design does a huge amount of work in making combat readable and intense.

Conclusion
Darktide is a frustratingly brilliant game. At its core I do feel it has one of the best first-person combat systems ever made. The blend of melee and ranged combat, the weight of every weapon, the movement, and the soundtrack all keep me coming back. It falls short due to poor performance, too few maps, underwhelming cosmetic support, and new modes that do not reach the heights of Vermintide 2’s wonderful Chaos Wastes.

And I keep coming back. Few games make moment-to-moment combat feel this good.

If you enjoy any two of the following: Left 4 Dead, Vermintide, or just the Warhammer 40,000 setting, you’ll very probably enjoy Darktide.

This game fill in a niche that is not for everyone, but if you are interested in a melee horde game this is the best out there.

Blessed be the cogitators. Blessed be the Tech-Priests who coded these long nights of purgation. Blessed be the servers of Fatshark, who in their toil for the Machine God have wrought something worthy of the name grimdark.

I have spent 1,143 hours in the underhive of Tertium upon the ash-choked world of Atoma, and I have not yet tired of the slaughter. That, by itself, is a miracle worth recording in the annals. Let this review stand as a hymn of praise — and, Emperor-willing, a thing of use to any Rejects still deciding whether to descend.

At first glance, this is a simple thing — a shooter, a game of trigger and blade. Heresy of a thought. Beneath the surface hums a machine of terrible complexity, classes each a cathedral unto itself, and within each class a dozen further heresies of build, loadout, and blessing to explore. I have played not one, but all, and still I find new catechisms to learn. The Omnissiah rewards those who study; the game punishes those who do not. This is as it should be.

The melee and ranged war-craft weave together in a manner few dare attempt — a hybrid liturgy of blade and bolt that looks, to the unschooled eye, like button-mashing chaos. It is not. Positioning, timing, the sacred rhythm of block and cleave and reload — these are disciplines, and the game teaches them slowly, cruelly, and fairly. Every death is a lesson from the Machine Spirit itself, and I have thanked it even as I bled out on the deck plating.

The atmosphere is a triumph of the Adeptus Mechanicus' own craft. Every corridor drips with grime and prayer-strips and the incense of promethium. Every limb parted from its heretical owner by shotgun-blast is rendered with a care that borders on reverent — as though the artists themselves were once executioners, and are pleased to remember the work.

And the sound! Omnissiah bless the sound engineers above all others. I no longer need eyes to know a beast has marked me for its own — the audio cue sings through the bone before the mind catches up. The clawed abominations that stalk the vents, the baying of the maddened mutant-things down some unseen hall — the sound travels, bends around the claustrophobic dark of these corridors, and tells a practiced ear whether death comes for me or for my brother-Reject beside me. This is craftsmanship few games achieve and fewer still bother attempting.

The dialogue between my fellow Rejects is a gift I did not expect to treasure as I do. With so many classes, so many voices, so many barks and quips and gallows-humor exchanges, no two squads sound quite the same, and the characters needle and jest at one another as though truly bound by shared damnation. I have laughed aloud in the dark more times than I can number — the mark of writing far better than this genre demands, and better than most bother to deliver.

And the score — Jesper Kyd's work here is a rite unto itself, dread and grandeur woven together so well I have stopped and simply listened more than once, forgetting the horde still baying at my back.

Last, and perhaps most sacred of all — the lore holds. Hive Tertium, sprawled across the world of Atoma, feels lived-in and true to the grim dark future the tabletop has spent decades building. Nothing here feels like a licensed skin slapped over a generic shooter. It feels like Warhammer. It feels like the Imperium as it has always been imagined — filthy, doomed, and magnificent.

One thousand, one hundred and forty-three hours, and I will gladly give a thousand more. To the Overseers at Fatshark: the Omnissiah's blessing upon your work, and upon every line of code that let a Reject like myself find so much joy in so much death.

The Emperor Protects. The Omnissiah Provides.

In true fatshark fashion, the game went from "Don't buy" at launch, to "pretty decent" 1-2 years later, to "one of the best Coop games I ever played". 
If you're into 40k and action/coop games this game is for you. If you like crafting different builds on a bunch of different character-classes who all have unique skill-trees and a variety of different weapons with blessings (weapon enchantments) this game is for you.

[b] Positives  [/b]

- Satisfying gameplay: The guns feel amazing. The melee combat is a dream. Most weapons have different versions of themselves (called "Marks") with varied movesets. At surface level with most weapons you can light attack, heavy attack, special attack, push attack, and sometimes sprint attack. All of these combat maneuvers can be interwoven and mixed up and reward players learning the specific moveset of their chosen weapon. In addition you can block, dodge, slide, jump, sprint and vault over smaller obstacles. Mastering movement and positioning becomes a crucial skill if you choose to play on higher difficulties. If you don't want to learn the intricacies of the combat system and just want to crush heretic skulls with a Thunder Hammer, you can do that too. There are lots of difficulty settings, it doesn't have to be a difficult game if you don't want it to be.

- Fatshark supports their games for a long time. Over the years lots of new content was added (both paid and free) and the recent developer notes about the patch (May 11, 2026) make it clear to me, that they care about the longevity of this game. They are actively trying to reign in some of the powercreep which seemingly always happens over the years in these kind of games when new content is introduced.

[b] Negatives / Critical points to keep in mind before buying: [/b]

- The game is quite CPU heavy and doesn't like AMD GPUs! There have been numerous reports of graphic- and framerate-issues with AMD cards over the years. Be sure to do some research before buying! If you have solid CPU (Intel or Ryzen both worked fine for me) and a semi old NVIDIA GPU (I still run a GTX 1660) you'll be fine.

- Microtransactions for skins. This isn't inherently bad but the microtransactions in this game are predatory imo. First: you can't buy them directly. You can only buy a special currency in predetermined amounts, trough which you can then buy the skin (obfuscating prices and generating "leftover, wasted" currency which is of course by design so you want to buy more afterwards... otherwise it'll go to waste...right??? - Press F to spit.) Second: The pricing is ridiculous and they blatantly use FOMO mechanics to psychologically manipulate susceptible people into buying their desired skin NOW. There is a "rotation" of skins in the shop creating artificial scarcity and it is undisclosed when and if a certain skin will reappear for purchase again.

[b] Conclusion: [/b]

One of the best coop action games there is. I'm biased though because I also love their other popular coop game "Vermintide 2", which is quite similar. 
BUT... avoid the "Commodores Vestures" microtransactions store like the plague (unless you're a paypiggy and get off on being abused)
